sections.body_md:
Feedback can make the sensitivity small on a band you care about, and it cannot make it small on every band at once. For a stable open loop that falls off at least as fast as \(1/\omega^2\), the signed area of \(\ln|S|\) from zero frequency out to infinity is zero. A dip below 1 is paid for by a hump above 1. That trade is the limitation.

Right-half-plane poles and zeros cut the same budget from two other directions. A right-half-plane pole has to be stabilized, which wants the crossover high enough. A right-half-plane zero cannot be cancelled by a stable compensator, and it wants the crossover low enough that its phase has not yet been spent. A delay spends phase in proportion to frequency and tightens the same ceiling.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
When the closed loop is stable and \(|L|\) falls at least as \(1/\omega^2\),
\[
\int_0^{\infty} \ln|S(j\omega)|\,d\omega = \pi \sum_k \mathrm{Re}(p_k),
\]
with the sum over the right-half-plane poles of the loop. No such poles means the integral is 0. At an uncancelled right-half-plane zero \(z\) of the loop, \(L(z) = 0\), so \(S(z) = 1\). The design window used in one of the questions, crossover at least twice a real right-half-plane pole and at most half a real right-half-plane zero, is a stated gap, not a replacement for the integral.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A single real right-half-plane pole at \(1.7\ \mathrm{rad/s}\) makes the integral \(\pi \times 1.7\), about 5.341. That area is positive, so \(\ln|S|\) cannot be negative everywhere: somewhere \(|S|\) exceeds 1 by enough to pay the 5.341. Separately, suppose the integral is zero, \(|S| = 0.4\) on a band of width 3.5, and the hump is allowed to reach 3.2. The hump width is \(-\ln(0.4)\times 3.5 / \ln(3.2)\), about 2.757. A narrower hump would have to be taller than 3.2.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The factor in front of the pole sum is \(\pi\), not \(2\pi\), and it multiplies real parts, not the imaginary parts of a complex pair. A right-half-plane zero does not add a term to this integral; people who add \(\pi z\) are copying the pole formula onto the wrong singularity. Cancelling that zero with a right-half-plane compensator pole hides an unstable mode, so the interpolation \(S(z) = 1\) is the stable reading. And a hump width is a ratio of logarithms. Using the magnitudes themselves, without the log, balances the wrong areas.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A robust-performance weight that asks \(|S|\) to be small on a wide band can demand more negative area than the integral contains. The spec is then impossible for every stable proper compensator, before any uncertainty weight is drawn. Robust stability still has to be checked on its own test. The delay that spends the phase in this budget is modeled apart from the integral, as a unit-magnitude block whose phase is \(-\omega\) times the delay.
